old: This word once described a sea so still that sailors barely noticed it moving — until people mistook its Latin roots for meaning the opposite of that stillness.
In Spanish, it could mean fair weather, dead calm, or a rich vein of ore before English borrowed it for sudden fortune.
Its transformation was nudged by the Latin word for 'good' — the same root behind English's own 'bonus.'
clues: This noun for a stroke of great good fortune began as something far less thrilling: its ancient Latin ancestor simply meant a calm sea.
It means a sudden, abundant source of wealth or profit, richer and longer lasting than a single windfall. In Spanish it could also mean a rich lode of ore.
Headlines hail a record weekend as a box office one. Its reshaped form was influenced by Latin bonus, meaning good, which also gives English the word bonus.
